paper_title: Let Samples Sing in Chorus: Mitigating Spurious Correlations via Cross-view Consensus

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that fail on underrepresented groups. Existing methods either correct human-specified bias attributes or infer unknown biases from the learned representation space. However, annotated attributes may differ from the shortcuts actually used by a model, while a single representation provides incomplete and potentially noisy evidence. Our key insight is that a bias obscured in one feature space may be clearer in another. In this work, we propose CHORD (Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing), a multi-view framework that allows samples to "sing in chorus" across diverse representation spaces to achieve robust cross-view consensus. CHORD aggregates aggregates within-class partitions in each view, which is a proxy for specifying candidate biases, to debias the target representation and classifier without bias supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks across vision, language, speech, and medical imaging show consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/davelee-uestc/chord_debiasing_public .

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that fail on underrepresented groups. Existing methods either correct human-specified bias attributes or infer unknown biases from the learned representation space. However, annotated attributes may differ from the shortcuts actually used by model, while single representation provides incomplete and potentially noisy evidence. Our key insight is that bias obscured in one feature space may be clearer in another. In this work, we propose CHORD (Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing), multi-view framework that allows samples to sing in chorus across diverse representation spaces to achieve robust cross-view consensus. CHORD aggregates aggregates within-class partitions in each view, which is proxy for specifying candidate biases, to debias the target representation and classifier without bias supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks across vision, language, speech, and medical imaging show consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ davelee-uestc/chord_debiasing_public. 1. Introduction Deep neural networks often exploit spurious features that are highly correlated with the label for most training samples but fail on underrepresented groups [17, 40]. For example, biased model may recognize birds by their backgrounds rather than their appearance, performing well on majority groups such as waterbirds on water, but misclassifying bias-conflicting samples in minority groups such as waterbirds on land. Similarly, it may diagnose diseases from medical devices rather than the pathology itself *Corresponding author. [7, 36, 53]. Many previous methods address this problem using predefined spurious attributes or group annotations from human experts [25, 39, 47]. However, annotation is costly, and the annotated attribute may not be the one the model actually uses. Models can favor features that differ from human expectations due to their architectures [16] or even random initializations [2]. Removing humanannotated spurious attribute therefore does not guarantee that the model bias is removed. Recent methods instead discover bias from the model to be debiased (the target model) itself due to its modeldependent nature. Existing methods use signals such as errors [31], losses [34], and gradients [12] to identify biasrelated samples. However, these signals can mix with label noise or intrinsic task difficulty, making it difficult to distinguish such effects from failures caused by spurious correlations. Representation-based methods instead seek readily available spurious features that models tend to learn, but require assumptions about the target geometry: GEORGE relies on separable subclasses [43]. NSF relies on strong spurious features producing identifiable within-class deviations [28]. Such methods keep discovery tied to the target model, which is constrained by the its geometry. When spurious feature is entangled with semantic variation or artifacts of geometry, the pattern found is noisy estimate of the bias: it may still cover most bias-conflicting samples, yet they are diluted by unrelated ones. As in empirical risk minimization (ERM), the corrective signal can remain too weak to counter the majority pattern, leading to poor worstgroup accuracy (WGA), the lowest accuracy across groups. Our starting point is simple: noisy candidate bias pattern in one representation may be denoised in another. Models trained with different objectives organize the same samples differently and emphasize different attributes [16, 20]. spurious attribute that is difficult to disentangle from noisy cofounder in the target representation may therefore pro1 duce clearer within-class division in another representation, which we call view. This can potentially provide less noisy candidates for correcting the target model. Because all views observe the same samples, the candidate can be transferred through sample identities, without aligning feature spaces or naming the underlying attribute. Bias discovery can thus benefit from structures that are more visible outside the target representation. Based on this insight, we propose Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing (CHORD), multi-view debiasing framework that requires no group annotations. Unlike prior methods constrained by the target geometry, CHORD decouples where candidates are proposed from where they are validated: candidates come from several views of the same samples, while validation stays in the target space. It proceeds in three phases: each view proposes candidate bias, the target representation validates it, and the evidence from all views are aggregated for debiasing. Two design choices make this possible. First, CHORD represents each candidate bias as within-class partition, allowing views to communicate their hypotheses through sample assignments without aligning feature spaces or specifying bias attributes. Second, CHORD filters views by testing every partition in the target space, since an auxiliary view, like human annotator, may highlight attributes that are not the spurious cue to remove from the target features. The test uses constrained transformation to suppress feature differences between the two subsets and keeps samples whose nearest-centroid assignments return to their labeled class. These reversal samples provide correction evidence from the partition. Each view decides where to look, while the target representation determines what views to keep and what samples contribute to debiasing. The evidence obtained from all views is aggregated into soft sampling weights for retraining the classifier head. Auxiliary views are frozen during training, and discarded at inference. We evaluate CHORD on seven benchmarks spanning vision, language, and speech, with multiple architectures. On the four standard benchmarks, CHORD achieves the highest WGA among the compared methods without bias supervision. We further explore constructing views from heterogeneous modalities in the Discussion section. Our contributions are as follows. We propose CHORD, multi-view debiasing framework that decouples where biases are proposed from where they are tested. This allows bias discoverying on multiple representations, relaxing reliance on the target geometry. We represent candidate biases as within-class partitions, providing transferable proxy that connects different representation spaces through sample assignments without feature alignment or predefined bias attributes. We evaluate CHORD on seven benchmarks with multiple target architectures, showing highest WGA among competing methods without bias supervision. 2. Related Work Mitigating Spurious Correlations. Spurious correlations allow models to exploit dataset-specific shortcuts that fail under distribution shifts [17, 46]. Existing methods broadly follow two routes: specifying bias information or inferring it through assumptions about learning behavior. The former includes group-supervised robust optimization [39] and estimating missing spurious-attribute labels from limited annotations [35]. Prior knowledge also guides interventions against texture dependence [16, 19, 33], counterfactual image generation [41], and methods that use language models to improve robustness [1]. However, annotations are costly, and the specified attributes may not cover the shortcuts used by particular model; suppressing one shortcut can even amplify another [29]. The other route reduces dependence on explicit bias labels by constructing deliberately biased auxiliary models [6, 34] or exploiting simplicity bias [45]. Initial-model errors or confidence [31, 38] and pseudo-bias labeling [22] provide signals for emphasizing bias-conflicting samples. Data-level approaches instead create or expose alternative training signals through biastailored swapping [24], bias-adversarial augmentation [30], or masking discriminative regions [4]. Although these interventions differ, their effectiveness depends on how well the supplied or inferred bias matches the target models tendency to learn spurious features. Learning-based proxies may also reflect ordinary task difficulty or noise, motivating bias discovery grounded in the target model without predefined bias attributes or group annotations. Representation-Based Bias Discovery and Mitigation. Learned representations support both lightweight correction and direct bias analysis. DFR [25] and AFR [38] exploit useful information retained by biased encoders through last-layer retraining, while contrastive objectives reshape feature relationships across bias conditions [21, 54]. Information-theoretic regularization also discourages shortcut dependence in dense prediction [10, 11]. For discovery, clustering-derived pseudo-attributes guide debiased learning [42], and FACTS [52] amplifies correlations before discovering bias-conflicting slices in feature space. NSF [28] uses within-class geometry; ShortcutProbe [55] identifies latent prediction shortcuts; and Evidential Alignment [51] uses uncertainty and evidence calibration to characterize and mitigate model bias. Related approaches train diverse predictive hypotheses to explore alternatives to shortcut solutions [27, 44]. Within this literature, representationbased bias discovery remains sensitive to its own geometry. Hermann et al. [20] show that the features model uses depend on both their predictive value and their availability, where availability refers to how easily they can be extracted from inputs. This motivates considering differences in at2 tribute visibility across representations: variation that is insufficiently prominent for discovery in the target space may be more accessible in another representation. CHORD uses pretrained and geometry-enhanced views to supply candidate partitions, reducing reliance on the target geometry that spurious variation being sufficiently prominent. The candidates are evaluated in the target space, so the additional views broaden the sources of evidence while keeping bias discovery tied to the model being corrected. 3. Proposed Method 3.1. Overview CHORD decouples proposing candidate biases from testing them for more reliable bias discovery. bias pattern estimated from the target features alone may mix the spurious split with semantic variation, noise, or artifacts of the target geometry. We therefore propose candidates from several representations of the same samples and test each one in the target feature space. Discovery can thus draw on multiple sources and reduce the impact of noise from any single source, while the test stays tied to the model being corrected. 3.2. At inference, CHORD retains only the target encoder f0, target transformation t0, and updated classifier head h. The auxiliary encoders and transformations {tv}v=0 are used only during training. 4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Settings Datasets. We evaluate CHORD on three tasks. Vision. Waterbirds [39] contains 4,795 landbird and waterbird images with spuriously correlated backgrounds. CelebA [32] contains over 200,000 face images; we predict hair color and define groups by gender. CheXpert [23] contains over 200,000 chest radiographs; we adopt the binary task and group construction of SubPopBench [50]. Language. MultiNLI [49] contains 412,349 labeled sentence pairs labeled as entailment, contradiction, and neutral; negation terms is the spurious attribute. CivilCommentsWILDS [26] contains 448,000 comments labeled as toxic or non-toxic, with groups defined by demographic identity. Speech. For emotion recognition, CREMA-D [8] provides 7,442 recordings from 91 actors across six emotions. We evaluate five attributes: sex, binary race, median-split age, age quartiles, and the intersection of sex and binary race. Sex, binary race, and binary age each define 12 emotionattribute groups; age quartiles and sexrace intersections each define 24 groups. For MEAD [48], we use fixed subset of 31,729 recordings from 48 actors across eight emotions. The actor-disjoint training, validation, and test splits contain 21,125, 5,302, and 5,302 recordings from 32, 8, and 8 actors, respectively. We evaluate groups defined by emotion and either speaker sex or emotional intensity. Metrics. We report test mean accuracy (mAcc) and worst-group accuracy (WGA). For CREMA-D and MEAD, we average the attribute-specific WGAs over five and two group definitions, respectively; individual and intersectional results appear in the multi-attribute analysis. All CHORD results use the last-epoch checkpoint. Network Architecture. Image tasks use ImageNetpretrained ResNet-50 [18]; Waterbirds and CelebA additionally use ViT-B/16 [15] for cross-architecture evaluation. Language tasks use BERT-base-uncased [14], and speech tasks use fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0-base [5]. Implementation Details. All experiments use PyTorch [37] on an Nvidia GeForce 3090 GPU. Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods We compare against JTT [31], MT [4], CNC [54], AFR [38], EA [51], SP [55], GDRO [39], DFR [25], NSF[28], and uLA [47] on the four popular benchmarks under the same group definitions. As shown in Tab. 1, CHORD obtains the highest WGA among methods without bias or group supervision on all four benchmarks, increasing their mean WGA from 82.01% for NSF to 84.49%. We report both mAcc and WGA to expose their tradeoff. 4.3. Results on Speech Emotion Recognition We evaluate the method on CREMA-D and MEAD using wav2vec 2.0. As shown in Tab. 2, CHORD improves WGA over the paired ERM models by 7.39 on CREMAD and 4.49 on MEAD. For reference, GDRO trains one expert per evaluation attribute, five on CREMA-D and two on MEAD. We average each experts mAcc and its WGA under the matched evaluation attribute. GDRO chooses different expert for each evaluation attribute. We therefore report it as an attribute-matched oracle reference, not as the performance of single model under all attribute definitions. Under this, CHORD exceeds GDRO by 7.82 in WGA on CREMA-D and 5.55 on MEAD, using single model trained without attribute annotations. 4.4. Cross-Architecture Applicability We further examine whether the method depends on particular target architecture. Table 7 compares ERM and CHORD using both ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 on Waterbirds and CelebA. These results show that CHORD improves worst-group accuracy over ERM with both architectures. 4.7. Robustness Across Attribute Definitions Multiple Post-Hoc Attributes CREMA-D allows us to evaluate the same trained model under five post-hoc group definitions covering sex, race, two age discretizations, and the intersection of sex and race. As shown in Tab. 8, CHORD improves WGA over ERM under all five definitions, although none of these attributes is used by the method during training. Against ERM, the largest improvement occurs under age-quartile grouping, where CHORD raises WGA by 11.89. These results support simultaneous robustness to multiple possible group definitions, rather than the stronger claim that each latent bias is separately recovered or assigned to particular view. We also evaluate five GDRO models trained with different group annotations for reference, each under all five evaluation attributes. Underlined entries are the attribute-matched GDRO results. CHORD results are averaged over 10 classifier seeds on fixed ERM features; GDRO uses one model seed per attribute. Age-B/Q denote binary/quartile age groups; SexRace denotes sex race. CHORD achieves highest WGA under all five definitions without attribute-specific training. METHOD Train attr. mAcc WGA by evaluation attribute Sex Race Age-B Age-Q SexRace Mean ERM CHORD 77.08 62.00 61.54 62.50 52.63 77.11 66.70 69.62 69.41 64.52 GDRO 75.92 59.41 62.32 61.32 55.10 Sex 74.04 55.56 57.89 60.49 53.49 Race 77.08 63.37 63.08 64.15 55.56 Age-B Age-Q 76.54 58.59 62.32 65.26 57.89 SexRace 76.54 60.40 62.32 62.50 57.14 59.46 64.86 59.38 48.44 56.67 51.56 56.67 59.63 67.02 59.51 55.17 60.57 59.12 59.81 Table 9. Attribute-role exchange on CelebA to assess transfer across prediction tasks. Blond Hair and Gender exchange their roles as the prediction target and evaluation attribute, using the standard ResNet-50 CHORD configuration without task-specific retuning. We report means over 10 random seeds, with WGA standard deviations. CHORD improves WGA under both assignments. ERM CHORD TARGET EVAL. ATTRIBUTE mAcc WGA mAcc WGA Blond Hair Gender Gender Blond Hair 95.60 47.20 90.78 89.060.50 98.64 87.22 97.73 96.030.51 out task-specific retuning. As shown in Tab. 9, CHORD attains 89.06% WGA for Blond Hair prediction and 96.03% for Gender prediction, without accessing the evaluation attribute during training. For the exchanged task, CHORD improves WGA over its matching ERM checkpoint by 8.81. This test evaluates transfer across attribute roles; it does not imply that the two attributes are simultaneously recovered as separate latent biases. 5. Discussion Transformations & Random Views. On CelebA, we keep the ERM model and the final transformation fixed, averaging 10 classifier seeds and, for randomized views, 10 independently sampled partitions. Target-only achieves 82.39% WGA; adding one random view with 50% or 25% withinclass outliers yields 83.20%/83.84%. Removing the transformation from reversal checking or using original centroids yields 64.67%/80.09%, with the final transformation unchanged. In separate experiment, we add one CLIP view using three partition variants: the original partition, partition with half of its outliers replaced by inliers, and fully randomized partition. With batch size and training steps fixed, auxiliary candidates must be target outliers; we then enable or disable the reversal check. Enabling it changes WGA from 85.90%/84.38%/77.10% to 85.90%/85.06%/83.42%, respectively, supporting the checks utility under corrupted partitions. Strong performance with random candidates also shows the contribution of target-space test; the small originalrandom gap here should be distinguished from the comparison with all pretrained partitions randomized below. Randomizing all pretrained partitions. We replace all six pretrained partitions with independent random partitions, matching each views outlier count within each class. The target partition, final transformation, update budgets, and geo admission (off) remain fixed. On CelebA, across 10 independent randomizations. Pretrained versus random partitions yield 89.060.50% versus 75.281.25% WGA. Both standard deviations are across classifier seeds, with random results first averaged over randomizations per seed. ERM seeds. On CelebA, CHORD achieves 88.60 0.47% WGA across three ERM seeds, versus 82.91% for target-only; each ERM result averages 10 classifier seeds, and the standard deviation is across ERM means. Beyond in-modality views. Since view only produces within-class partition, it need not share the targets modality or even observe the input directly. This opens two possibilities. First, views can be built through language: Image VLM Caption BERT z(v) partition qv, (4) captioning CelebA images with VLM then encoding with BERT improves WGA by 1.5 over target-only. Because captions can be steered by prompts, this also offers natural channel for human priors to coexist with automatic discovery. Second, views can be borrowed from another modality: Speech log-Mel Spectrogram DINO z(v) partition qv. (5) on MEAD, rendering speech as log-Mel spectrograms and encoding them with frozen DINOv3, raises WGA from 50.77 to 52.04 and contributes 22 reversal samples not found from the target view alone. These results suggest that CHORD can draw on representation views beyond pretrained encoders of the target modality, which also mitigates the scarcity of such encoders in specialized domains. Extensible partition proposals. Replacing relativedistance partitioning with ERM errors in the target view and linear-probe (LP) errors in auxiliary views, we follow the main-experiment CHORD training recipe. CelebA WGA improves from 44.39% with direct partition-balanced retraining to 82.33% with target-only CHORD and 84.50% with auxiliary proposals, demonstrating extensibility beyond the choice of representation views. Computation. On one GeForce 3090, CHORD takes 4.5/13.9 on Waterbirds/CelebA from cache loading to the first trained classifier while competing methods JTT and CNC require minutes to hours[38]. Timings exclude ERM training and feature extraction; 8 Limitations. CHORD requires recoverable core features in the frozen target representation and restricts reversal evidence to the target-outlier pool. Although CHORD is evaluated on multiple tasks, suitable pretrained encoders may be less available in specialized domains. In such settings, CHORD can still combine the target representation with its geometry-enhanced view or heterogeneous views. 6. Conclusion This work introduces CHORD, framework for mitigating spurious correlations without group annotations. CHORD separates proposing candidate biases from testing them: multiple views propose within-class partitions, and the target model tests each partition through reversal samples. This design rests on simple observation: spurious cues are shaped by the target representation, but evidence of them can come from outside the target model. Experiments on benchmarks across vision, language, speech, and medical imaging consistently demonstrate improved worstgroup accuracy.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: OpenAI Codex was used to assist with drafting and revising manuscript text, including the Introduction, Related Work, and Limitations, and with literature lookup and LaTeX preparation. It also assisted with code preparation, experiment execution, and result checks. The authors remain responsible for the scientific claims, experimental results, and final manuscript.
